title: WHY JONATHAN ATE THE HONEY WHEN AN ENTIRE ARMY WAS FASTING
paragraphs:
WHY JONATHAN ATE THE HONEY WHEN AN ENTIRE ARMY WAS FASTING
One Taste Opened His Eyes—and Exposed Something Terrifying About the Kind of Religion That Can Exhaust People While God Is Trying to Give Them Victory
There was honey on the ground.
Imagine that scene.
Thousands of exhausted men. Weapons in their hands. Dust on their faces. Adrenaline draining from their bodies. Stomachs empty. Legs weakening.
And honey was right in front of them.
Not hidden.
Not locked away.
Not across enemy lines.
Right there.
Yet no one touched it.
Men who were brave enough to charge armed Philistines were afraid to put food into their mouths.
Then Jonathan walked into the forest.
He saw the honey.
He extended his staff.
He dipped its end into the honey.
He tasted it.
And something happened that Scripture describes with a remarkably vivid Hebrew expression:
"וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו"
vatta'ornah einav.
“And his eyes brightened.”
—1 Samuel 14:27
That tiny moment raises an enormous question.
Why was Jonathan eating when the entire army was fasting?
Was he rebellious?
Was he disrespecting authority?
Was this some mysterious biblical endorsement of breaking a fast?
No.
And if we rip this scene away from its context, we can make it say things God never said.
Jonathan was not secretly sneaking food because he disagreed with his father.
Scripture explicitly tells us:
"וְיוֹנָתָן לֹא־שָׁמַע בְּהַשְׁבִּיעַ אָבִיו אֶת־הָעָם"
VeYonatan lo-shama behashbia aviv et-ha'am.
“Jonathan had not heard when his father made the people swear.”
—1 Samuel 14:27
Jonathan ate because he did not know about Saul's oath.
That detail matters.
But what happened after he ate reveals something even deeper.
Because this story is not primarily about honey.
It is about what happens when human zeal begins masquerading as spiritual wisdom.
It is about leadership that can sound religious while crushing the people underneath it.
And eventually, it points us toward our desperate need for a better King.
Go backward a few verses.
Before Saul ever commanded the army not to eat, Jonathan had already done something astonishing.
Israel was facing the Philistines.
Jonathan looked at his armor-bearer and essentially said: Let's go.
Two men.
Against an enemy outpost.
His confidence was not in numbers.
Listen carefully to his theology:
"כִּי אֵין לַיהוָה מַעְצוֹר לְהוֹשִׁיעַ בְּרַב אוֹ בִמְעָט"
“For nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.”
—1 Samuel 14:6
There is Jonathan.
Then there is Saul.
Jonathan moves because God is powerful.
Saul imposes an oath because Saul wants revenge.
That difference is easy to miss.
Saul said:
“Cursed be the man who eats food until evening, before I have avenged myself on my enemies.”
Notice the language.
“My enemies.”
“My revenge.”
The battle belonged to the LORD, but Saul's language was becoming painfully centered on Saul.
And while Saul was trying to intensify Israel's pursuit through an oath, the result was the opposite.
The soldiers became weak.
The Hebrew text later describes them as:
"וַיָּעַף הָעָם מְאֹד"
Vayya'af ha'am me'od.
The people were exceedingly faint, exhausted, famished.
The king demanded more.
The soldiers had less strength to give.
Then Jonathan tasted a little honey.
His eyes brightened.
Suddenly he understood what the exhausted army could not say.
“My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.”
Then Jonathan makes the painfully practical observation that if the soldiers had been permitted to eat from the enemy's spoil, Israel's victory could have been even greater.
Think about that.
Saul's command was apparently intended to strengthen the pursuit.
Instead, it weakened the pursuers.
And then things became worse.
The starving soldiers eventually became so ravenous that they rushed upon the spoil and ate meat improperly with the blood, violating God's command.
Do not miss the irony.
A man-made restriction intended to intensify religious commitment helped create circumstances in which exhausted people rushed into actual disobedience.
That does not mean biblical fasting is wrong.
Far from it.
Scripture presents genuine fasting as a meaningful expression of humility, repentance, mourning, prayer, and seeking God.
Jesus Himself fasted.
Jesus taught about fasting.
The early church fasted.
The problem in 1 Samuel 14 was not simply “fasting.”
This was Saul's oath imposed upon soldiers in the middle of battle, under threat of a curse, tied explicitly to Saul's desire for vengeance before evening.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sometimes people read this story and conclude:
“Jonathan teaches us to break religious rules.”
No.
That is not what happened.
Jonathan had not heard the oath.
And there is another dangerous interpretation we should reject.
The honey was not some magical substance that spiritually enlightened Jonathan.
The phrase “his eyes brightened” describes the reviving effect of nourishment on an exhausted man.
Jonathan ate.
His strength returned.
His condition visibly changed.
But there is something haunting about the image nevertheless.
An entire army walked past provision because they were terrified of a curse spoken by their king.
Jonathan tasted what they feared to touch...
and his eyes brightened.
Maybe that image feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to become exhausted in the name of religion.
You prayed.
Served.
Gave.
Volunteered.
Stayed quiet.
Tried harder.
Smiled at church.
Quoted Scripture.
Told everyone you were blessed.
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary, you became spiritually exhausted.
Not because Jesus was cruel.
Not because God's Word failed.
But because somewhere along the road, human expectations became tangled together with God's commands.
And eventually you could no longer tell the difference.
Someone told you that being tired meant you lacked faith.
Someone made their personal conviction sound like God's universal command.
Someone used fear where Scripture offered grace.
Someone demanded performance but rarely spoke of the finished work of Christ.
Maybe that person was a leader.
Maybe it was your family.
Maybe it was an entire religious culture.
Or maybe...
it was you.
Maybe the harshest Saul in your life has sometimes been the voice inside your own head.
“Do more.”
“God must be disappointed.”
“Try harder.”
“You haven't prayed enough.”
“You haven't sacrificed enough.”
“You aren't spiritual enough.”
“You failed again.”
And slowly Christianity stops feeling like knowing Christ and starts feeling like desperately trying to convince Christ not to reject you.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say, “Exhaust yourself until God finally loves you.”
The Gospel says God loved sinners so profoundly that He gave His Son.
The Gospel does not say, “Perform well enough and perhaps your debt will disappear.”
Jesus said from the cross:
“Τετέλεσται.”
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
—John 19:30
Finished.
Not “almost finished if you can complete the rest.”
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
This is where Jonathan's story must ultimately drive the Christian heart—not toward Jonathan as our savior, but toward Jesus Christ as the King Jonathan could never be and Saul tragically was not.
Because Scripture gives us another King.
Saul burdened exhausted men for the sake of his victory.
Jesus carried the burden Himself for the sake of His people.
Saul pronounced a curse that endangered his own son.
Christ willingly bore the curse to rescue His enemies.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
—Galatians 3:13
Saul was prepared to let his son die because of a rash oath.
The Father gave His Son according to His eternal saving purpose so sinners could live.
That difference is everything.
Jesus does not lower God's holiness.
He fulfills righteousness.
Jesus does not pretend sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves how terribly sin matters.
Grace is not God shrugging at your rebellion.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
And that means repentance is not an enemy of grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
You don't repent so Jesus will become merciful.
You repent because the crucified and risen Jesus is the only refuge sinners have.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness you've learned to justify.
An affair happening mostly through messages—but you know where your heart has gone.
Pride dressed like discernment.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Gossip renamed “concern.”
A prayer life disappearing behind endless scrolling.
A Bible collecting dust while your phone knows every movement of your thumb.
Maybe you're not running from church.
You attend every Sunday.
You're just running from surrender.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that nobody around you knows.
You know the songs.
You know when to raise your hands.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know Christian language well enough to hide inside it.
But Jesus does not want the edited version of you.
He already knows the unedited one.
And still the invitation of the Gospel stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Stop hiding behind your performance and bring your actual sin to the actual Savior.
There is another detail in Jonathan's story that becomes almost unbearable.
Saul eventually discovered that Jonathan had eaten.
He was prepared to kill him.
Jonathan—the man whose faith had helped ignite Israel's victory—stood under a death sentence because of an oath he had never even heard.
Then the people intervened.
They refused to let Jonathan die.
But every human rescue in Scripture leaves us longing for the rescue only Christ can accomplish.
Because unlike Jonathan, we cannot stand before God and say:
“I didn't know.”
We have sinned knowingly too.
We have crossed lines with our eyes open.
We have ignored convictions.
Broken promises.
Returned to sins we swore we would abandon.
Loved things God told us to leave.
Failed people who trusted us.
And if our only hope were our innocence...
we would have no hope.
But Christianity announces something far better than the innocence of the sinner.
It announces the righteousness of Christ.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace that finds guilty people and changes them.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that disciplines.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that can take the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read and refuse to let that chapter become the final sentence of your life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never happened.
But by taking repentant sinners and writing redemption where condemnation once seemed inevitable.
Perhaps that's why the honey in Jonathan's hand still speaks so vividly thousands of years later.
One exhausted man tasted provision...
and his eyes brightened.
But there is a sweetness infinitely greater than honey.
The psalmist said of God's words:
“How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!”
And the Gospel tells us those words ultimately lead us to a Person.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your soul isn't starving because God abandoned you.
Maybe you've been trying to survive spiritually on everything except Christ.
Approval.
Religious performance.
Entertainment.
Relationships.
Money.
Sex.
Recognition.
Ministry.
Even theology can become a hiding place if knowing information about Jesus replaces actually walking with Jesus.
Your soul was never designed to live on applause.
It was never designed to live on dopamine.
It was never designed to live on people's approval.
You were created for God.
And no amount of earthly honey can satisfy a heart that was created to know its Creator.
What is starving inside you?
What have you been pretending isn't there?
What are you afraid Jesus will expose if you finally become completely honest with Him?
Bring that thing into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need prettier religious language.
You need Christ.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need the cross.
You need the empty tomb.
You need the Holy Spirit changing what willpower alone could never transform.
And if this exposed something you've been hiding, don't write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer struggling.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally stop pretending because you stopped pretending first.
And if this article made you think of one particular person, don't just think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
Someone smiling in their profile picture may be barely holding onto faith.
Someone who would never walk into a church might read something a friend shared at 2:00 in the morning.
It isn't.

You glorify God through Jesus Christ by loving Him, obeying His Word, loving your neighbor, living faithfully, proclaiming the Gospel, serving others, giving generously as God leads, and using what He has entrusted to you for His purposes.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the King.
Jonathan tasted honey and his eyes brightened.
But when a sinner truly sees the grace of God in the face of Jesus Christ, something far greater begins.
The hiding can end.
The striving for acceptance can end.
The excuses can end.
The old master can lose its grip.
A sinner can repent.
A prodigal can come home.
A wounded believer can rise again.
A scandal can become a testimony of grace.
Because perhaps the most dangerous kind of starvation is having provision in front of you while believing you are forbidden to receive it.
And perhaps someone reading this tonight needs to discover that the arms of the crucified and risen Christ are still open to repentant sinners.

You may remember Jonathan for the honey—but never forget the Savior whose grace is sweeter, whose cross went deeper, and whose mercy can still rewrite the chapter you thought had ruined your story forever.
